= Development Mode & Debugging
:description: Running and debugging a GWT 2.13 application during development: Super Dev Mode and its CodeServer (port 9876, -src, -launcherDir, incremental compiles, the Dev Mode On and Off bookmarklets), source-map debugging in the browser devtools and an IDE, DevMode today (-noserver, -startupUrl, the static-file-only server), classic Dev Mode as history, the code server security caveat and troubleshooting.
:keywords: GWT, Super Dev Mode, SDM, CodeServer, DevMode, gwt:codeserver, gwt:devmode, launcherDir, bookmarklet, source maps, incremental compile, noserver, startupUrl, StaticResourceServer, GWT.log, GWT.debugger, classic Dev Mode, hosted mode, troubleshooting

include::partial$gwt-disclaimer.adoc[]

This page is written against GWT 2.13.1, `gwt-maven-plugin` 1.3.0 (`net.ltgt.gwt.maven`), a JDK 21 toolchain with `-sourceLevel 17`
and Jakarta Servlet 6 on the server side (Jetty 12 EE 10), and was checked on 2026-10-08; the code server and DevMode runs
shown here were executed on that stack with the Bookshelf scratch application. It is about **build and tooling** code, the
compiler process you keep running while you write **client** code, and how it cooperates with your **server** code. The
application sources themselves are unchanged by anything below, except for the optional `GWT.log` and `GWT.debugger` calls in
the debugging section.

== The development loop at a glance

A GWT application is Java that is compiled to JavaScript, so there are two questions during development: how do you see
a change without a full production compile, and how do you debug code that the browser runs as JavaScript. Since GWT 2.7
the answer to both is **Super Dev Mode** (SDM):

* a separate Java process, the **code server**, compiles your modules on demand in draft mode and serves the result;
* the browser loads that output instead of the deployed output, and you debug it in the browser devtools through
  **source maps** that point back to your `.java` files;
* your own server (Jetty, Tomcat, Spring Boot) serves the host page and the RPC or REST endpoints exactly as in production.

The same pieces exist under several names, and the official documentation still mixes them:

.Development tools and their status in GWT 2.13.1
[cols="1,2,2",options="header"]
|===
|Tool |What it is |Status

|`CodeServer` (`com.google.gwt.dev.codeserver.CodeServer`, artifact `gwt-codeserver`)
|The Super Dev Mode compiler and web server, a plain Java program. `mvn gwt:codeserver` runs it.
|The recommended tool. This is what the rest of the page is about.

|`DevMode` (`com.google.gwt.dev.DevMode`)
|A Swing window plus an optional embedded web server that starts the code server for you (`-superDevMode` defaults to on).
|Still shipped. Since 2.13.0 its embedded server only serves static files, and using it as an application server is deprecated.

|Classic Dev Mode (browser plugin, `-nosuperDevMode`)
|Ran the Java bytecode in the JVM and drove the browser through a plugin.
|Deprecated in 2.8.0, history only (see below).

|Hosted mode (`GWTShell`)
|The name of classic Dev Mode in the early GWT versions.
|Gone. The official FAQ still carries a note that "Hosted mode" and "web mode" were renamed development mode and production mode.
|===

Source: https://www.gwtproject.org/doc/latest/DevGuideCompilingAndDebugging.html#SuperDevMode[GWT -- Compiling and Debugging: Super Dev Mode]

== How Super Dev Mode works

The code server is an ordinary Java program with an embedded Jetty 9.4 web server (the GWT 2.13.1 BOM manages 9.4.58). It
does not run your client code in the JVM: it compiles the whole module to JavaScript, as the production compiler does, but in
draft mode with most optimizations off. That is why the core guarantee of old Dev Mode, "the Java ran the same as the
JavaScript", is replaced by a simpler one: what you debug is the compiled JavaScript, shown to you as Java.

[mermaid]
....
sequenceDiagram
  participant B as Browser
  participant H as Host server (Jetty on 8081)
  participant C as CodeServer (127.0.0.1:9876)
  participant J as Compiler (draft mode, incremental)
  B->>H: GET /bookshelf/bookshelf.nocache.js
  H-->>B: stub script written into launcherDir
  B->>C: GET /recompile-requester/bookshelf
  C-->>B: recompile script
  B->>B: confirm that the code server is ready
  B->>C: GET /recompile/bookshelf with the binding properties
  C->>J: compile only what changed since the last compile
  J-->>C: new output directory (compile-N)
  C-->>B: JSON status ok, or failed with the old output kept
  B->>C: GET bookshelf.nocache.js and the .cache.js files
  B->>C: GET the source map and the .java files on demand
....

Reading the diagram from the top: the page asks the host server for the module's `bookshelf.nocache.js`. The `-launcherDir`
output directory holds a small **stub** in that place, so the request reaches the code server, which recompiles if any source
changed and answers with the real bootstrap script. Without a `-launcherDir` you do the same by hand with the bookmarklets
(next section). When a compile fails, the code server logs the errors and continues to serve the previous version.

The article states the same thing from the other side: Super Dev Mode "replaces the internals of Dev Mode" and, because it
needs no plugin, works in modern browsers and on mobile browsers. It requires the `xsiframe` linker, which has been the
default since GWT 2.7, so a current module needs no configuration for it.

Source: https://www.gwtproject.org/articles/superdevmode.html#Introduction[GWT -- Super Dev Mode: Introduction]

== Starting the code server

=== With Maven

With `gwt-maven-plugin` the goal is `gwt:codeserver`. It is an **aggregator goal**: according to the plugin documentation, its
configuration lives in the **root POM**, not in the `gwt-app` module, and it runs the code server for the `gwt-app` modules of
the reactor. The `modular-webapp` archetype used by the Bookshelf scratch application generates this configuration in the
root POM:

[source,xml]
----
<plugin>
  <groupId>net.ltgt.gwt.maven</groupId>
  <artifactId>gwt-maven-plugin</artifactId>
  <inherited>false</inherited>
  <configuration>
    <launcherDir>${basedir}/bookshelf-server/target/gwt/launcherDir</launcherDir>
    <!-- To be able to use gwt:devmode (useful on Windows where Ctrl+C won't kill gwt:codeserver)-->
    <warDir>${basedir}/bookshelf-server/target/gwt/launcherDir</warDir>
    <devmodeArgs>
      <arg>-noserver</arg>
    </devmodeArgs>
  </configuration>
</plugin>
----

Source: https://tbroyer.github.io/gwt-maven-plugin/codeserver.html#Running_and_debugging[gwt-maven-plugin -- Running and debugging]

Three details are worth knowing. The goal puts the sources of the reactor modules that you depend on as `gwt-lib` or with the
`sources` classifier on the code server's source path as they are, so an edit in `bookshelf-shared` is picked up without
rebuilding it. Dependencies use the `runtime` scope by default (`classpathScope`), where `gwt:compile` uses `compile`. And because
the code server takes different arguments from the compiler, an option that both need, such as a custom
`-setProperty`, has to be given twice, in `compilerArgs` for the production compile and in `codeserverArgs` for the code server.

The plugin documentation recommends limiting the reactor to client modules so that the server is not built on every start:

[source,bash]
----
mvn gwt:codeserver -pl bookshelf-client -am
----

Source: https://tbroyer.github.io/gwt-maven-plugin/codeserver.html#Running_and_debugging[gwt-maven-plugin -- Running and debugging]

The real output of this command on the scratch application (JDK 21, GWT 2.13.1, plugin 1.3.0; the middle of the Maven log is
omitted):

[source,text]
----
[INFO] --- gwt:1.3.0:codeserver (default-cli) @ bookshelf ---
[INFO] Turning off precompile in incremental mode.
[INFO] Super Dev Mode starting up
[INFO]    workDir: .../app/target/gwt/codeserver
[INFO]    Loading Java files in com.example.bookshelf.App.
[INFO]    Module setup completed in 1651 ms
  [WARNING] ...:INFO:oejs.Server:main: jetty-9.4.58.v20250814; ...
  [WARNING] ...:INFO:oejs.AbstractConnector:main: Started ServerConnector@...{HTTP/1.1, (http/1.1)}{127.0.0.1:9876}
[INFO] The code server is ready at http://127.0.0.1:9876/
----

Source: https://tbroyer.github.io/gwt-maven-plugin/codeserver-mojo.html[gwt-maven-plugin -- gwt:codeserver]

The `[WARNING]` prefix on the Jetty lines is only the Maven plugin forwarding the forked process's standard error; they are
informational. The code server turns off `-precompile` itself ("Turning off precompile in incremental mode", printed by its
`Options` class) because an incremental compile works on one permutation, as explained below.

The same goal has `launcherDir`, `logLevel`, `style`, `sourceLevel`, `failOnError`, `modules`, `projects`, `jvmArgs` and
`codeserverArgs` parameters. On the scratch application, `codeserverArgs` containing `-port 9886` was placed in the
**client** module's POM and had no effect (the server still started on 9876) because the aggregator goal reads its
configuration from the root POM, so put any port change there.

=== Without Maven

Run `com.google.gwt.dev.codeserver.CodeServer` from `gwt-codeserver` with `gwt-dev` and the application classpath, giving at
least one module name. This is the 2.13.1 argument list as printed by the class itself:

[source,text]
----
CodeServer [-[no]allowMissingSrc] [-[no]compileTest] [-compileTestRecompiles count] [-[no]failOnError]
  [-[no]precompile] [-port port] [-src dir] [-workDir dir] [-launcherDir]
  [-bindAddress host-name-or-address] [-style (DETAILED|OBFUSCATED|PRETTY)]
  [-setProperty name=value,value...] [-[no]incremental]
  [-sourceLevel [auto, 1.8, 9, 10, 11, 17]]
  [-logLevel (ERROR|WARN|INFO|TRACE|DEBUG|SPAM|ALL)] [-[no]generateJsInteropExports]
  [-includeJsInteropExports/excludeJsInteropExports regex]
  [-XmethodNameDisplayMode (NONE|ONLY_METHOD_NAME|ABBREVIATED|FULL)]
  [-X[no]closureFormattedOutput] [module]
----

Source: https://www.gwtproject.org/articles/superdevmode.html#Starting[GWT -- Super Dev Mode: Without Dev Mode]

Run with no module, the program prints the line `Usage: at least one module must be supplied`. The flags that matter every day:

.CodeServer flags (GWT 2.13.1)
[cols="2,3,2",options="header"]
|===
|Flag |Purpose |Default

|`-port`
|The TCP port of the code server.
|`9876` through the Maven goal and DevMode

|`-src`
|A directory of GWT source prepended to the class path used for compiling. Repeatable. Under Maven the plugin passes one per source root.
|none

|`-launcherDir`
|The directory into which the files for launching Super Dev Mode, including the stub `+*.nocache.js+`, are written.
|none (use the bookmarklets)

|`-workDir`
|The root of the tree where the code server writes compiler output (`compile-1`, `compile-2` and so on).
|a temporary directory

|`-bindAddress`
|The address for the code server and its web server.
|`127.0.0.1`

|`-[no]incremental`
|Reuses data from the previous compile.
|on

|`-[no]precompile`
|Compiles the modules once when the server starts.
|on, switched off by the code server when incremental

|`-style`
|Script style: `DETAILED`, `OBFUSCATED` or `PRETTY`. `PRETTY` gives readable names in stack traces.
|`OBFUSCATED`

|`-setProperty`
|Fixes a deferred-binding property, for example `user.agent=safari`, to reduce the permutations.
|none

|`-[no]failOnError`
|Stop if any input file has an error, even if unused.
|off

|`-sourceLevel`
|The Java source level. The help text and the Developer Guide are right: the default is 1.8 (a default argument registered in `ToolBase`). Java 12-17 syntax needs an explicit `-sourceLevel 17`, and `auto` resolves to the level of the running JVM.
|1.8

|`-[no]allowMissingSrc`
|Allows `-src` to name directories that do not exist yet.
|off

|`-[no]compileTest`, `-compileTestRecompiles`
|Compile (and recompile) once and exit with status 0 on success. Useful in a continuous-integration check that the code server can build the module.
|off
|===

Source: https://www.gwtproject.org/articles/superdevmode.html#Starting[GWT -- Super Dev Mode: Without Dev Mode]

== Triggering a recompile: bookmarklets or launcherDir

There are two ways to tell the browser "use the code server's build of this module". Both end up in the same state: the
original `+*.nocache.js+` of the page finds a redirect and loads the code server's output.

=== Bookmarklets

When you start the code server without `-launcherDir`, you compile and deploy the application once, serve its host page from
your own server, and then open the code server page (`http://127.0.0.1:9876/`). It lists two bookmarklets, **Dev Mode On**
and **Dev Mode Off**, to drag onto the bookmarks bar. On your application page click *Dev Mode On*, pick the module and press
*Compile*: the code server compiles the module, stores its URL in the page's session storage and reloads the page. The page's
own `bookshelf.nocache.js` finds the entry and redirects to the code server's copy:

[source,javascript]
----
window.sessionStorage["__gwtDevModeHook:bookshelf"]
// returns "http://127.0.0.1:9876/bookshelf/bookshelf.nocache.js"
----

Source: https://www.gwtproject.org/articles/superdevmode.html#HowItWorks[GWT -- Super Dev Mode: How the bookmarklet works]

The key is stored in session storage, so it is per browser tab and disappears when the tab is closed. *Dev Mode Off*
removes it and the page returns to the deployed output. The compile button in the dialog is itself a bookmarklet that can be
dragged to the toolbar.

=== The launcherDir approach

With `-launcherDir` the code server writes a stub `bookshelf.nocache.js` into that directory. If you make the directory part
of your web application (the archetype's `env-dev` profile adds it as an extra Jetty resource base, and
`gwt:codeserver` and `gwt:devmode` both write to it), the host page's script tag loads the stub instead of the real
bootstrap. The stub inserts the code server's recompile script at the top of the page head, and that script asks the code
server to recompile on every page reload. Its source is short; the relevant part of the file written on the scratch
application reads:

[source,javascript]
----
var hostName = $wnd.location.hostname;
var serverUrl = 'http://' + hostName + ':9876';
var module = 'bookshelf';
var nocacheUrl = serverUrl + '/recompile-requester/' + module;
----

Source: https://tbroyer.github.io/gwt-maven-plugin/codeserver.html#Running_and_debugging[gwt-maven-plugin -- Running and debugging]

and, if the script cannot be loaded, it shows a confirm dialog:

[source,text]
----
Couldn't load bookshelf from Super Dev Mode
server at http://localhost:9876.
Please make sure this server is ready.
Do you want to try again?
----

Source: https://github.com/gwtproject/gwt/blob/main/dev/codeserver/java/com/google/gwt/dev/codeserver/stub.nocache.js[GWT repository -- stub.nocache.js]

The two approaches compare as follows:

.Bookmarklets versus launcherDir
[cols="2,3,3",options="header"]
|===
|Aspect |Bookmarklets |launcherDir stub

|Setup
|Drag two bookmarklets once per browser.
|One path in the build; nothing in the browser.

|Reload behaviour
|After *Dev Mode On* the page recompiles when you press *Compile* in the dialog or the bookmarklet.
|Every page reload asks the code server to recompile and waits for the result.

|Host page needs
|A deployed build of the application (its `+*.nocache.js+` does the redirect).
|Nothing deployed: the stub is the module's bootstrap in development.

|Works for
|Any server, including one you do not control.
|A server that can serve the launcher directory as static resources.

|Danger
|None specific.
|The stub must never reach production (see the security section).
|===

== Incremental compiles

Draft-mode compiling alone would still take seconds per change. SDM adds **incremental compilation**
(`-incremental`, on by default): the code server keeps a rebuild cache of the compiled types and, on the next compile, only
re-traverses types that depend on a changed source file. The release notes add that it also caches this data on disk, which
speeds up the first compile after a restart.

Incremental compilation compiles **one permutation** per request. The bookmarklet or the stub sends the browser's actual binding
properties (the `user.agent` and `locale` that deferred binding would choose), so the code server compiles exactly the
permutation your browser will run. The first request in the scratch application, issued by hand without those properties,
shows what happens when the properties expand to more than one permutation:

[source,text]
----
[INFO] GET /recompile/bookshelf
[INFO]    Job com.example.bookshelf.App_1_0
[INFO]       starting job: com.example.bookshelf.App_1_0
[INFO]       binding: user.agent=safari
[INFO]       Current binding properties are expanding to more than one permutation but incremental compilation requires that each compile operate on only one permutation.
[INFO]       0,022s total -- Compile completed
----

Source: https://www.gwtproject.org/articles/superdevmode.html#HowItWorks[GWT -- Super Dev Mode: How the bookmarklet works]

With both properties given (`locale` and `user.agent`) the first compile of the Bookshelf, which has three locales and two user
agents, succeeded and the next edit of one string was recompiled much faster:

[source,text]
----
[INFO] GET /recompile/bookshelf
[INFO]       binding: locale=en
[INFO]       binding: user.agent=safari
[INFO]          Unification traversed 26992 fields and methods and 2568 types. 2527 are considered part of the current module ...
[INFO]             Linking per-type JS with 2506 new/changed types.
[INFO]             Source Maps Enabled
[INFO]          Compilation succeeded -- 9,149s
[INFO]       9,375s total -- Compile completed
(after changing one @DefaultMessage string)
[INFO]       binding: locale=en
[INFO]       binding: user.agent=safari
[INFO]          Unification traversed 1103 fields and methods and 844 types. 8 are considered part of the current module ...
[INFO]             Linking per-type JS with 8 new/changed types.
[INFO]          Compilation succeeded -- 0,485s
[INFO]       0,563s total -- Compile completed
----

Source: https://www.gwtproject.org/doc/latest/DevGuideCompilingAndDebugging.html#SuperDevMode[GWT -- Compiling and Debugging: Super Dev Mode]

The first compile took 9.1 s, the incremental one 0.56 s with 8 changed types instead of 2506. A request with no change at
all is answered without compiling (`skipped compile because no input files have changed`, 13 ms). A restart of the code
server is faster than the first start because of the on-disk cache (3.9 s for the same module in the last run). Times are from a
laptop and only meant as orders of magnitude.

To shorten the cold compile, narrow the permutations for development with `-setProperty`, or in a development module with
`set-property` (for example `user.agent` fixed to the browser you use). The module-XML side of that is covered on
xref:web/gwt/compiler-and-compilation.adoc[Compiler & Compilation].

== Debugging in the browser with source maps

Because SDM runs JavaScript, you debug it in the **browser's devtools**. The compiler emits a source map (`Source Maps
Enabled` appears in the compile log; since 2.12.0 source maps are on in all browsers), and the compiled `.cache.js` ends with a
`sourceMappingURL` comment that points to the code server:

[source,text]
----
//# sourceMappingURL=http://127.0.0.1:9876/sourcemaps/bookshelf/DF97226FAEF9B2B2AA29587BF7177179_sourcemap.json
----

Source: https://www.gwtproject.org/articles/superdevmode.html#HowSourceMapsWork[GWT -- Super Dev Mode: How sourcemap-based debugging works]

The devtools then request the Java files themselves from the code server, so the *Sources* panel shows `+com/example/bookshelf/client/...+`
files you can set breakpoints in. The article describes the URL shape; on the scratch application:

[source,bash]
----
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:9876/sourcemaps/bookshelf/com/example/bookshelf/client/App.java
----

Source: https://www.gwtproject.org/articles/superdevmode.html#HowSourceMapsWork[GWT -- Super Dev Mode: How sourcemap-based debugging works]

returned the file after the first compile (the status code is 200 with `Content-Type: text/plain`) and a 404 with the page message
`+This module hasn't been compiled yet.+` before it. This is also the first sign of the security caveat below: the source of the
module is served to whoever asks.

Plan your debugging session around what SDM is and is not:

* **Breakpoints and stepping** in the Java files work. The article recommends Chrome, where support is best, and notes that you
  may have to enable source maps in the devtools settings.
* **Variables** are JavaScript values: the field names and values you see in the scope panel are those of the compiled code,
  not Java ones.
* **No JVM checks.** SDM does not run the application in a JVM, so some runtime checks do not happen; the article gives the array
  index out of bounds as an example. The production compile can also turn off or reduce checks that SDM's draft build still
  performs, so run a production build before release.
* **Logging.** `GWT.log` writes to the browser console in SDM (and is removed from production output). `GWT.debugger()` emits a
  JavaScript `debugger` statement that stops when the devtools are open, with no effect in server code. The Javadoc for the
  shared `GWT` class documents both; `java.util.logging` can be routed to the console as well (see xref:web/gwt/logging.adoc[Logging]).

The following change to the Bookshelf presenter uses `com.google.gwt.core.shared.GWT` rather than the client class, so that the
presenter stays unit-testable in a plain JVM; the module compiled under the code server with the two calls, and the string
`Loading books` is present in the compiled output.

[source,java]
----
import com.google.gwt.core.shared.GWT;

public void load(int start, int length) {
  GWT.log("Loading books " + start + ".." + (start + length));
  service.getBooks(start, length, new AsyncCallback<BookPage>() {
    @Override
    public void onSuccess(BookPage page) {
      display.showRows(start, page.getBooks(), page.getTotal());
    }

    @Override
    public void onFailure(Throwable caught) {
      GWT.log("getBooks failed", caught);
      GWT.debugger(); // stops here when the browser devtools are open
      display.showError(caught.getMessage());
    }
  });
}
----

Source: https://www.gwtproject.org/doc/latest/DevGuideCompilingAndDebugging.html#generating_debug_messages[GWT -- Compiling and Debugging: Generating debug messages]

Never log secrets, session tokens or whole user records with `GWT.log` or `System.out` even in development: console output
reaches screenshots, bug reports and browser extensions. Remove any `GWT.debugger()` before merging; it is harmless to users with
closed devtools but is a leftover that makes a production page stop for anyone who opens them.

== Debugging from an IDE and the server side

No official page documents an IDE-specific procedure for SDM, so only the general shape is given here.

* **Client code.** An IDE that can attach to the browser's JavaScript debugger and honours source maps can set breakpoints in
  `.java` files in the same way the devtools do, because the maps and the sources both come from the code server URL. This is a
  feature of the IDE, not of GWT, and works only while the code server is running.
* **Shared and server code.** Code in the `shared` module that is also compiled for the JVM, and everything in the server
  module, runs in an ordinary JVM, so a normal Java debugger attached to the servlet container (or to `mvn jetty:run`) works
  as always. Attach with the JVM's standard `-agentlib:jdwp` option in `MAVEN_OPTS`, or use your IDE's Maven or Spring Boot run
  configuration with Debug.
* **Presenters and plain Java.** The best IDE debugging experience for client logic remains a JUnit test of a presenter whose
  view and service are fakes (xref:web/gwt/testing.adoc[Testing] covers it); no code server or browser is needed.
* **The code server's own JVM.** To debug a generator or an annotation processor that runs inside the compiler, start the
  code server (or the Maven goal's forked JVM, `jvmArgs`) with a JDWP agent. This is rarely needed.

The tutorial in the official documentation debugs StockWatcher in an IDE with classic Dev Mode ("Debug As" in Eclipse). That
procedure no longer applies to current GWT, and the Eclipse plugin text it relies on is historical.

Source: https://www.gwtproject.org/doc/latest/tutorial/debug.html[GWT -- Tutorial: Debugging]

== DevMode today

`com.google.gwt.dev.DevMode` is still shipped and still the main class of the old `ant devmode` and Eclipse launch
configurations. In 2.13.1 it is a thin shell around SDM, and its role changed in 2.13.0:

* **`-superDevMode`** is on by default (`ArgHandlerSuperDevMode.getDefaultValue()` returns `true`). Setting it to `-nosuperDevMode`
  is the deprecated classic mode.
* DevMode starts the code server by reflection (`SuperDevListener`); if `gwt-codeserver` is not on the class path the log says:
  `Unable to find main() method for Super Dev Mode code server. Hint: verify that gwt-codeserver.jar is in your classpath.`
* **`-[no]startServer`** (default on) starts an embedded servlet container for the directory given with `-war`.
  `-noserver` is a documented alias of `-nostartServer` in `DevModeBase`. With it you run your own server and DevMode only
  compiles and starts the code server.
* **`-startupUrl url`** adds a URL that DevMode offers to open ("Automatically launches the specified URL"); a URL without a
  host is taken as `localhost` and the embedded server's port.
* **`-port`** is the embedded web server's port (8888), **`-codeServerPort`** the code server's (9876 in SDM, 9997 for classic).
  **`-bindAddress`** defaults to `127.0.0.1`.
* **`-war`**, **`-deploy`**, **`-extra`**, **`-workDir`**, **`-style`**, **`-setProperty`**, **`-incremental`** and **`-sourceLevel`**
  work as for the compiler and the code server.

DevMode opens a Swing window. Started with `-Djava.awt.headless=true` on the scratch application with `-noserver`, it fails
before doing anything else:

[source,text]
----
java.lang.RuntimeException: Error running on Swing UI thread
	at com.google.gwt.dev.SwingUI.invokeAndWait(SwingUI.java:411)
	...
Caused by: java.awt.HeadlessException
----

Source: https://github.com/gwtproject/gwt/blob/main/dev/core/src/com/google/gwt/dev/DevMode.java[GWT repository -- DevMode.java]

That makes DevMode unsuitable for servers, containers and CI. `mvn gwt:codeserver`, which has no GUI, is the replacement, and
the plugin keeps `gwt:devmode` only for standalone applications that have no server of their own (client code only, or CORS
to an API). For those, point `startupUrls` at a host page from the module's public path.

=== The 2.13 static-file-only server

Up to 2.12, `-startServer` launched an embedded Jetty that also ran your servlets from `WEB-INF` (so you could serve RPC from
DevMode). The 2.13.0 release notes changed the default:

[quote, GWT 2.13.0 release notes, https://www.gwtproject.org/release-notes.html#Release_Notes_2_13_0]
DevMode server defaults to only serving static files.

The default server class is now `StaticResourceServer`: a Jetty `ResourceHandler` that serves the `-war` directory and
nothing else (no servlets, no `web.xml`). The previous launcher is still present, selected with
`-server com.google.gwt.dev.shell.jetty.JettyLauncher`, but the release notes describe it as "due to be removed", and the 2.11
notes had already deprecated "using DevMode as an application server". The official advice is to split the client and server
class paths, or to implement a `ServletContainerLauncher` that runs another server (the notes link a sample project that
does this), or simply to run your servlet container separately.

[source,bash]
----
# DevMode with the legacy launcher (not recommended, due to be removed)
java -cp "$CP" com.google.gwt.dev.DevMode \
  -server com.google.gwt.dev.shell.jetty.JettyLauncher \
  -war target/gwt/launcherDir \
  -startupUrl index.html \
  com.example.bookshelf.App
----

Source: https://www.gwtproject.org/release-notes.html#Release_Notes_2_13_0[GWT -- Release Notes 2.13.0]

The `-server` flag takes `servletContainerLauncher[:args]`, either a fully qualified class or the name of a
`ServletContainerLauncher` registered with the Java `ServiceLoader`. Specifying `-server` overrides `-noserver`.

For a real servlet container or Spring Boot application, which is what the Bookshelf uses, none of this is needed: run the
server as you do in production (here the Maven Jetty plugin with `-Denv=dev` so the launcher directory is served) and run
`gwt:codeserver` beside it.

[source,bash]
----
# terminal 1: the client side, recompiles on demand
mvn gwt:codeserver -pl bookshelf-client -am

# terminal 2: the server side (Jetty 12 EE 10 with the launcher directory as an extra resource base)
mvn -pl bookshelf-server -Denv=dev org.eclipse.jetty.ee10:jetty-ee10-maven-plugin:12.1.10:run -Djetty.http.port=8081
----

Source: https://www.gwtproject.org/doc/latest/DevGuideCompilingAndDebugging.html#use_my_own_server_in_development_mode_instead_of_GWT[GWT -- Compiling and Debugging: Using my own server in development mode]

Open `http://localhost:8081/` and the browser asks the code server (on 9876) for the module. A Spring Boot server works the same
way as long as it serves the launcher directory as a static resource location in its development profile; the GWT side does not
care which server delivers the host page. The same arrangement is the answer to the DG section on EJBs: GWT provides the
code server or the `-noserver` option for that case.

== Classic Dev Mode and the plugins: history only

Before GWT 2.7 (and still in the 2.x documentation text), development mode meant the JVM executing the Java bytecode of your
client code, connected to a regular browser through a **browser plugin** (the GWT Developer Plugin), with the Java debugger
of the IDE attached to that JVM. It gave full Java debugging, and the DevMode window showed a log tree with `GWT.log` messages,
a *Restart Server* button for the embedded Jetty, and the `-logLevel SPAM` option for the engine's internal messages. The
approach needed a plugin per browser. The 2.8.0 release notes list classic Dev Mode under deprecations (with a
temporary switch back, `+gwt.args='-devMode'+`, for test cases), and since 2.7 launching DevMode starts Super Dev Mode. A modern application cannot use the plugin; its
remnants are the flags `-nosuperDevMode` and
`-codeServerPort 9997` and the screenshots of the Swing window in the older text.

The first edition of the Manning book _GWT in Action_ (Hanson and Tacy, 2007; it targets GWT 1.3 and 1.4) describes the earlier
hosted mode, a launcher class `GWTShell` with an embedded browser and Tomcat, for debugging in an IDE; that is the ancestor of the
mechanism above and none of its procedures, class names or screenshots apply to GWT 2.13. Everything it says about breakpoints in
client Java belongs to the pre-Super-Dev-Mode era.

Source: https://www.gwtproject.org/release-notes.html#Release_Notes_2_8_0[GWT -- Release Notes 2.8.0]

== Security: the code server must never be exposed

The Super Dev Mode article is explicit that the code server has no authentication and hands all of your Java source code to
anyone who asks, and therefore recommends running it only on localhost or behind a firewall. In the code (`WebServer.java`) every static response carries `+Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *+`, which was verified
on the scratch application:

[source,bash]
----
curl -s -D - -o /dev/null http://127.0.0.1:9876/bookshelf/bookshelf.nocache.js | grep -i access-control
# Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *
----

Source: https://github.com/gwtproject/gwt/blob/main/dev/codeserver/java/com/google/gwt/dev/codeserver/WebServer.java[GWT repository -- WebServer.java]

Treat the port as a development-machine-only interface:

* Keep the default `-bindAddress 127.0.0.1`. Do not bind to `0.0.0.0` or forward the port from a shared host, VM or container
  to a network you do not control: anyone who can reach it can read your sources through `+/sourcemaps/...+` and trigger
  compiles (including `/clean`, which wipes the disk cache). For testing from a phone, use a trusted network and shut the code
  server down afterwards.
* The article says that `https` is not supported (a referenced upstream issue is gwtproject/gwt#7535), so a host page served over
  `https` loads a script from an `http` origin, which browsers treat as mixed content and may block. Test with `http` hosts or
  use a browser setting for local development.
* **Never deploy the launcher directory or its stub `+*.nocache.js+`**. The stub names a code server on the page's host and port
  9876 and runs whatever script that URL returns. The production artifact is the output of `mvn package` (`gwt:compile`), not
  `target/gwt/launcherDir`. Keep the Maven `env-dev` profile, and any Spring Boot development profile that exposes the directory,
  out of production configurations.
* Source maps and the sources they reference are also sensitive when produced by a production compile. Whether to publish them
  is a deployment decision discussed on xref:web/gwt/linkers-and-bootstrap.adoc[Linkers & Bootstrap] and xref:web/gwt/xsrf-rpc-and-server-security.adoc[XSRF, RPC & Server Security].
* The code server and the Swing DevMode are development tools: they hold no user data, but they run your build, so run them as an
  unprivileged user and do not point them at untrusted modules.

== Worked example: Bookshelf development session

This session combines the pieces on the Bookshelf scratch application: the server, the code server, an edit, an error and the
recovery.

. Start the two processes as in the previous section, then open `http://localhost:8081/` in Chrome. The stub asks the code
  server to compile; the first compile of the application takes about 9 s (3.9 s on a warm disk cache).
. Open the devtools, choose *Sources* and press the search shortcut to open `CatalogPresenter.java`. Set a breakpoint on the
  `+service.getBooks(...)+` line and reload: the compile is skipped (nothing changed) and the breakpoint is hit.
. Change a string in `AppMessages.java` and reload. The log shows `Compiling 1 permutation`, 8 new or changed types and a
  half-second compile.
. Introduce a typo (an `int` after the `@DefaultMessage` annotation). The reload still shows the previous version, and the code
  server log shows the errors (below).
. Remove the typo and reload: the next compile succeeds and the page updates.

The failing recompile of step 4 answered the request with `+{"moduleNames":["bookshelf"],"status":"failed"}+` and logged:

[source,text]
----
[INFO]          Tracing compile failure path for type 'com.example.bookshelf.client.i18n.AppMessages'
[INFO]             [ERROR] Errors in 'file:.../bookshelf-client/src/main/java/com/example/bookshelf/client/i18n/AppMessages.java'
[INFO]                [ERROR] Line 6: The annotation @Messages.DefaultMessage is disallowed for this location
[INFO]                [ERROR] Line 7: Syntax error, insert ";" to complete FieldDeclaration
[INFO]                [ERROR] Line 7: Return type for the method is missing
[INFO]          [ERROR] Aborting compile due to errors in some input files
[INFO]       [ERROR] Compiler returned false
[INFO]       [WARN] recompile failed
[INFO]       [WARN] continuing to serve previous version
----

Source: https://www.gwtproject.org/articles/superdevmode.html#HowItWorks[GWT -- Super Dev Mode: How the bookmarklet works]

The last two lines explain the most common confusion of a new SDM user: after a compile error the browser keeps running the
last good build, so "my change does nothing" almost always means "read the code server's terminal". The browser's own
*Network* tab shows the failing `+/recompile/...+` response.

== Troubleshooting and pitfalls

.Common problems with the development loop (GWT 2.13.1)
[cols="2,3,3",options="header"]
|===
|Symptom |Cause |Fix

|A confirm dialog: `+Couldn't load bookshelf from Super Dev Mode server at http://localhost:9876. Please make sure this server is ready.+`
|The code server is not running yet, or listens on another host or port, or is bound to a different address than the page uses.
|Wait for `+The code server is ready at ...+`, start it, and reload. Open the page with the same host name (the stub builds the URL from `location.hostname`) that the code server is reachable at.

|My edit has no effect after a reload
|The recompile failed and the code server continues to serve the previous version (`recompile failed`, `continuing to serve previous version`).
|Read the code server terminal for `[ERROR]` lines and fix them; the page updates on the next successful compile.

|`GET /recompile/bookshelf` logs `Current binding properties are expanding to more than one permutation but incremental compilation requires that each compile operate on only one permutation.`
|A manual call (curl or a script) without the `user.agent` and `locale` properties, so the compile spans several permutations. A later request for the module's `bookshelf.nocache.js` then answers 500 with a `NullPointerException` in `Outbox.getOutputDir()` because no output exists yet.
|Let the stub or bookmarklet send the properties, or pass them yourself (`?user.agent=safari&locale=en`), or fix them with `-setProperty` or a development module.

|`+/sourcemaps/...+` returns 404 with `+This module hasn't been compiled yet.+`
|Devtools asked for a source before the first successful compile of this module.
|Reload the application page so that the first compile runs.

|Old behaviour persists after changing module XML, a `ClientBundle` or a generator, or the code server seems to use stale data
|The incremental cache and the on-disk cache hold compiled data from before the change.
|Open `http://127.0.0.1:9876/clean` (the response is `Cleaned disk caches.`), or stop the server and delete `target/gwt/codeserver`, then reload. The 2.8.0 notes mention an incremental-compile fix for changed compiler options, so keep options stable between starts.

|`port` set in the client POM is ignored
|`gwt:codeserver` is an aggregator goal; its configuration comes from the root POM.
|Put `codeserverArgs`, `launcherDir` and `logLevel` in the root POM's plugin configuration.

|`java.awt.HeadlessException` and `Error running on Swing UI thread`
|`DevMode` needs a display for its Swing window.
|Use `mvn gwt:codeserver` plus your own server.

|`Unable to find main() method for Super Dev Mode code server. Hint: verify that gwt-codeserver.jar is in your classpath.`
|`DevMode` runs `CodeServer` by reflection and `gwt-codeserver` is not on the class path.
|Add `org.gwtproject:gwt-codeserver` (managed by the `gwt` BOM) or use the Maven goal.

|After switching to `-noserver` or your own server, RPC fails with a serialization policy error (see xref:web/gwt/gwt-rpc.adoc[GWT-RPC])
|The `*.gwt.rpc` serialization policy files in the module output are older than your serializable types. The Developer Guide notes that these files must be redeployed if the serializable types change.
|Recompile (the code server regenerates them) and serve the module output that the code server produces; do not copy a stale directory.

|The page does not use the code server at all
|The page's `+*.nocache.js+` is the production one and no bookmarklet was pressed, or session storage key was removed by closing the tab.
|Use the launcherDir stub, or press *Dev Mode On* again on the tab.

|Breakpoints in Java files never hit, or lines are off
|The browser did not apply source maps (disabled in the devtools settings), or the page runs a cached old build.
|Enable source maps in the devtools, hard-reload with the cache disabled, and check that the `.cache.js` ends with a `sourceMappingURL`.

|A bug appears only in the production build
|SDM compiles in draft mode and omits checks the JVM would perform. The Developer Guide states the principle that if it runs in development mode and compiles, it should behave the same, with rare exceptions.
|Run `mvn package` and test the result in the target browsers before release, with `-style PRETTY` if you need readable stack traces.

|`+-pl '*-client'+` fails with `Could not find the selected project in the reactor`
|Wildcard project selection is a Maven 4 feature; Maven 3.9 does not support it.
|Use `-pl bookshelf-client` or `-pl :bookshelf-client`.
|===

Source: https://www.gwtproject.org/doc/latest/FAQ_Troubleshooting.html[GWT -- FAQ: Troubleshooting]

== Where older material is outdated

* Articles and tutorials that start "development mode" with `ant devmode`, `webAppCreator` or an Eclipse launch configuration
  describe the classic flow. `webAppCreator` is deprecated and its generator classes were removed in 2.12.0, so a new project
  starts from a Maven archetype (see xref:web/gwt/getting-started.adoc[Getting Started] and xref:web/gwt/build-tools-maven-and-gradle.adoc[Build Tools: Maven & Gradle]).
* The Developer Guide page "Compiling and Debugging" still documents the DevMode options with the older defaults (the embedded
  Jetty serving your servlets, a GUI with a *Restart Server* button) and does not mention the 2.13 change; the release notes do.
* The `-sourceLevel` help text and the guide say the default is 1.8, which is correct for the command-line tools; the Java 12-17 features of 2.12.0 and later need an explicit `-sourceLevel 17` (the `auto` value resolves to the running JVM's level).
* The book's hosted mode and the plugin-based flow of 2.0 to 2.6 are historical, as above.
